questions.q: What does this lesson say a portfolio proves that a résumé line cannot?
options: It proves the architect has more years of experience than other candidates
It proves the architect has a Salesforce certification
It proves the architect's actual reasoning on a specific problem, which a reader can evaluate directly rather than taking on faith
Nothing — a portfolio and a résumé prove exactly the same thing
questions.explain: A résumé claim has to be taken on faith; a well-written case study lets the reader evaluate the actual reasoning directly (the tradeoffs named, the alternative considered), which is why it carries more weight in a technical hiring process.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say not every one of the course's eight cases belongs in every portfolio?
options: Because weaker cases should simply be deleted and never shown to anyone
Because case studies expire after six months and can't be reused
Because only exactly three cases are ever allowed in a portfolio
Because selecting cases is itself a design decision driven by what the specific audience needs to see, and padding with irrelevant cases dilutes the ones that actually matter
questions.explain: The lesson frames case selection the same way as requirements extraction in Lesson 9 — what does this specific audience need as evidence — and warns that including every case regardless of relevance dilutes the strength of the ones that actually matter for that audience.

questions.q: Why does the portfolio-readiness checklist require that a case name at least one risk or assumption, rather than presenting the design as risk-free?
options: Because a design with no visible downside reads as less credible, not more, to an experienced reviewer who knows every real design involves tradeoffs
Because risks are only relevant for Salesforce-specific designs, not general architecture
Because naming a risk guarantees the design will be approved
Because the checklist doesn't actually require this — it's optional
questions.explain: An experienced reviewer knows every real design has tradeoffs; a case presented as flawless reads as less thought-through, not more, which is why the checklist specifically requires at least one named risk or assumption.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about presenting one of the course's fictional case studies as if it were real client work?
options: It's recommended, since it makes the portfolio sound more impressive
It's a credibility risk that costs far more trust than the case would have earned, and honest framing as a practice case is the stronger, not weaker, approach
It doesn't matter either way as long as the reasoning is sound
Fictional cases should never be included in a portfolio under any framing
questions.explain: Misrepresenting a practice case as real client work risks far more credibility damage if discovered than the case would have earned. Honest framing as a deliberate practice exercise is explicitly presented as the stronger approach, not a weaker one.

questions.q: Per the checklist, what makes a written case meaningfully stronger than just "here's what we designed and why"?
options: Including as many technical acronyms as possible
Omitting any mention of alternatives considered, to keep the story simple
Stating an outcome or plausible follow-up, even for a fictional case, framed honestly as part of the exercise rather than fabricated as a real result
Making the case as long as possible regardless of relevance
questions.explain: "Here's what we designed, why, and what we learned once it was in use" is stronger evidence than just the design and rationale alone — and for a fictional case, that outcome can be stated honestly as part of the practice exercise without being presented as a real result.
